1:
Gill opens on the pause. Bildad was heard out without interruption, and when his oration closed Job rose in his own defence. Henry notices where that answer begins. Bildad had twice led with a How long (Job 8:2, Job 18:2), so Job, replying to him particularly, leads with a How long of his own — and with the better warrant, since a stronger case can be shown for defending ourselves, right being on our side, than for assaulting a brother. Keil and Delitzsch call it a justified quousque tandem: a man in unutterable agony, now racked by three assailants of united strength. Ellicott marks the same mirroring and names what provoked it, a personal malice infused into Bildad's last charges which the sufferer felt most keenly of all.

What is vexed is the soul, and Gill makes that the sting; the body may be vexed, but to be vexed to the very heart is worst. He catalogues what galls a godly man — corruptions that are as thorns in his side, the fiery darts of temptation, the talk of the profane that wearied righteous Lot — and ends where Job stands, galled by his own companions. Clarke is blunter. No kind word drops from the three at any point, none of them being touched with tenderness; the term friend must here mean a cold-blooded acquaintance, and posterity has by common consent handed them down to endless infamy.

Henry itemises the injury under six heads: they wounded his spirit, broke him in pieces with words, charged him with what he knew not, stood aloof in his trouble, grew big to make him small — a mean thing, trampling those already down — and worst of all pleaded his calamity against his uprightness, where they should have pleaded his uprightness against his calamity (2 Corinthians 1:12). Where, he asks, shall an honest man be found, if a bad name counts as evidence?

Nobody counts the ten strictly. Keil and Delitzsch call it round rather than exact; Clarke sends us to Genesis 31:7 for the idiom; Wesley has a certain number put for an uncertain. Gill canvasses and rejects the arithmeticians — Jarchi's ten paragraphs, Saadiah's pairing of speech with answer, the five orations each carrying a doubled slight — preferring Aben Ezra, that no tally is intended. Henry agrees on the sense yet turns it back on the speaker: to keep so exact a reckoning looks like a design of retaliation, and we serve our own peace better by letting injuries drop than by scoring them up. Clarke hears in the companion phrase the whole history of a reversal: in affluence they were his intimates and seemed glad of his happiness, and now they barely know him; circumstances change men's minds.

The concession that follows is granted for argument only. Gill will not have it taken as confession, though he allows a stumble in judgment, practice or speech, since who can understand his errors, and none is to be made an offender for a word. What the clause then secures is disputed. Gill and Henry hear a disclaimer of teaching: whatever the mistake, it is kept at home and not pressed on anyone else, which is the one thing that makes error tolerable. Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott hear instead a plea for pity — the harm falls on the one who erred, there is no public stain on his life, he alone smarts for it, and his companions neither sympathise nor suffer with him. Why then, Clarke asks, treat a man as though his life had been one general blot and his example a public curse? Gill's last note is the swagger they are warned against: to talk big, open the mouth wide with swelling words, and set what they call his error in the worst light it will bear.
6:
Everything here is laid at one door. Gill notes that Job has always ascribed his losses to God: whoever the instruments, it was God who cast him down from a high estate. The second verb, which may be rendered perverted, he fences carefully: God made him neither perverse in word nor crooked in act, nor twisted his cause, so Bildad's question whether the Almighty perverts justice gets a flat no. Clarke draws the practical inference: the matter lies between the sufferer and God, who commissioned nobody to add reproaches to his chastisements.

The net sets Clarke off on an antiquarian hunt. Read the clauses backwards, he says, and the figure is a mode of combat: the Roman netman with his trident against the swordsman, flinging his mesh over the head so that a noose tightened at the neck, obliged, if he missed, to run the ground until he had gathered it again. He adds the Persian loop thrown over a horseman and the Goths' hooped pole-net, citing Olaus Magnus; elsewhere he suspects the elephant pit of the previous chapter, or an invading army. Ellicott wants none of the machinery. Bildad had talked at length of the ungodly snared in his own sin; Job answers that substance without borrowing the words, choosing a different term for net and laying the hand that holds it on God.

Who has done the wrong is less agreed. Gill hears a complaint of violence — raiders on the herds, Satan on the body — cried as though in open court, a plain breach of justice. Clarke hears only the cry and its silence: injustice alleged, nobody coming to help. Wesley reads it of oppression by the three. Ellicott reads it of desertion by God, and tells us why the desolation is piled so high: the darker the forsaking, the greater the worth of the confession now coming, this severity having driven the man nearer to God and not away. He counts the heaped figures: assault unredressed, walls all round, a hope torn up like the tree of Job 14:7.

Gill works the blocked road as a traveller's image. The godly are pilgrims whose path, though rough, is commonly passable; sometimes it is hedged and they brush through scratched and torn; but at times a wall of hewn stone rises across it and they halt, not knowing which way to turn. The glory stripped he reads in a civil sense only — the magistrate's robe, the substance, the household, whatever made him magnificent among men — expressly not the robe of Christ's righteousness, which no plunderer touches. Wesley lists estate, children, authority and comfort, the crown standing for power and honour laid in the dust. Henry adds one item the rest miss, the opportunity of doing good, and reads the whole as worldly glory's vanity.

Henry sets the verses as three glances. Looking back, a hand has stripped him; looking down, the besiegers are God's own troops, lying about his tent as soldiers invest a city, cutting off supply and battering without pause, where once that encampment was a hedge of protection; looking forward, the road is walled and dark, with none to say how long. The uprooted tree he will not leave bare: hope in this life perishes, but a good man's hope, cut off here, is only transplanted from the nursery to the garden of the Lord, moved from sand to rock — which Wesley gives in almost the same words, where Clarke keeps it hopeless, a tree whose roots are out of the ground. Clarke alone strings the seven verses into one campaign, from unprovoked invasion to the storming of the royal city and the escape with the skin of the teeth; Keil and Delitzsch, counting thirty lines between the cry and the plea for pity, keep that stretch together as one block of verse.
13:
The circle of desertion is drawn from outside in, and the first question is whose hand draws it. Gill keeps the war figure: as a besieger cuts the defenders off from their allies, so every quarter from which comfort might come is held away. Henry divides the question. God laid on the affliction that frightened the kindred away and ordered their coldness toward the completing of the trial, but the coldness was their own sin and Satan's work, since he alienates men from a brother in trouble; every creature is to us what God makes it, which excuses nobody's ingratitude. Wesley states the rule in a line: look for the hand of God in the slights of friends as in the injuries of enemies. Gill adds that these brethren came at last, and showed brotherly love then.

Clarke reads the passage as a study in lost fortune. Reverenced once by all and esteemed now by none; many worship a rising sun who think little of one gone down, and some are reproached with the eminence they lost, though not to blame for losing it. He illustrates it with a bishop driven from his see under Queen Mary and never restored, greeted one morning with a pun on his title — Good morrow, Bishop quondam — answering, Adieu, Knave semper. Gill cares less for the moral than the household: the dwellers are not neighbours, as the Septuagint has it, nor tenants, but strangers taken in and given food and raiment as the law requires, or else proselytes; and he passes on Jerome's tradition that the house stood at Carnea, beyond Jordan.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the servant's silence by setting past against present: one who once read every order in his master's eyes and waited on his nod now neither comes at the call nor troubles to answer. Henry sharpens the reversal from the other side. Job never despised his servants' cause when they pleaded, and now they despise his; sick as he was he did not turn imperious but entreated where he might have commanded; nor should we wonder to get evil from those we have deserved well of. On the men of his counsel they work the Hebrew for a secret back to roots meaning to speak close or to be made impenetrable, so the phrase names those trusted with his most private plans — and they add, alone, that the clause about the loved turning against him is aimed at the three sitting before him. Gill, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley keep it general: intimates and confidants familiar with his affairs, not one of them respectful now.

What has turned strange to his wife is disputed. Gill offers a corrupt breath, then withdraws it shrewdly — were the smell so bad, the three could not have sat in the room through these long speeches — and prefers either his talk, unwelcome since he met her counsel to curse God by telling her she spoke like a foolish woman, or his very life, which wearied her. Henry makes the estrangement the price of that refusal. Ellicott repoints the next clause out of the quarrel altogether, reading it of Job's own kindness toward the children of his mother's womb, his brethren. Clarke keeps it literal and infers surviving younger children, too small for the feast where the rest died; he rejects the Septuagint's concubines as unsupported and quotes Coverdale instead. The mocking children are placed differently too: Gill has them outdoors, repeating what their parents taught, while Henry has them indoors, the servants' offspring and his servants by birth, who neither feared nor loved him when he rose to check them. Ellicott alone lifts the lament off Job, finding the Psalmist's verse copied from it and hearing throughout the accents of the Man of sorrows, in whom these words, and David's and Jeremiah's, are at home.
20:
The body comes first, and briefly. Gill observes the reversal: the bones once cleaved to the flesh, and now that the flesh is wasted they cleave to the skin and show through it, disease and grief between them leaving little else. Clarke takes the phrase about the teeth for a proverb of the narrowest escape — no thicker than the enamel — and says plainly it is a wonder the man lives. Keil and Delitzsch hear the change of register: strength and voice grow fainter, sadness replaces protest, and the address takes a tone of importunate entreaty meant, if anything can, to reach their hearts — they are his friends, after all, and the pronoun is emphatic. Ellicott calls it an exceeding great and bitter cry, the second of its kind here; Wesley locates the touch that drew it in the spirit, not the flesh, displeasure being the heaviest calamity of all.

All of them read the comparison that follows as a charge of usurped office. Gill makes it a question of standing: the Almighty answers to none, which men do, so his dealings are no precedent for ours — we are bound to be merciful as he is merciful, not licensed to harry his people because he has harried them for his own ends. He hunted Job as a lion hunts, which gave the three no warrant to join in; Gill notes a second rendering, where the clause asks why they hound him like one of the wicked lately described. Wesley makes the usurpation twofold: a claim to omniscience that searches a heart for hypocrisy, and a claim to the sovereign right of doing as one pleases. He gives the appetite in the next clause its teeth, likening them to beasts that will not devour prey without breaking the bones. Clarke asks whether what is sent is not already as much as a man can carry, and answers out of an English martyr's mouth at the stake, when a bystander flung a brand and split his face: why add this wrong? What the three assail is the spirit, the earlier blow having struck the body.

Then the complaint breaks off. Henry marks the abruptness and its reason: the man turns from grieving to triumphing, for others' edification as much as his own comfort, since those at hand would heed little and he wanted this kept for later generations. Henry has him disown his earlier outbursts — unadvised words he would rather see forgotten — and mark what comes next as deliberate: set in characters a runner could read, bound into a book, or cut into a monument with all the engraver's art. The wish was granted, he adds, the words standing in God's own book, told for a memorial wherever it is read; Wesley says the same in fewer words. Gill, Ellicott and Wesley agree that what is to be recorded is not the apology already made but the confession about to come, Ellicott resting that on the plain weight of the three verses following and perhaps on the word now.

Clarke turns the verse into a lecture on the history of writing, beginning with a correction of the translators: the verb means traced or described, not printed, printing being two thousand years off. Three methods are in view: a roll of papyrus or linen, one such drawn from an Egyptian mummy before his own eyes, an iron stile on lead sheets, and letters cut in rock, many surviving in Arabia. How the lead and the iron go together divides them. Gill argues for an iron stile writing on a leaden sheet, since lead leaves no lasting mark of its own and none at all on stone, and Clarke prefers the same; but Gill reports Jarchi's alternative, letters chiselled into rock with molten lead run into the grooves, which Wesley states as plain fact.
25:
Gill settles the grammar first: the opening particle is neither but nor for but nearer namely, so these three verses are what the preceding wish asked to have cut into rock. What follows is the most disputed passage in the book, and Clarke says so outright: more has been written on it than would fill the whole of Job printed in capitals. He lays down a premise neither party can do without: the speaker is under special inspiration and prophesying. Either reading needs it: no man of that age could speak unaided of a rising from the dead, and his restoration was as improbable. Weighing which revelation God would rather give, he takes the greater: a doctrine fit to govern wayward passions deserved so solemn a disclosure, where news the three would shortly witness anyway did not.

They divide on what is promised. Henry, Gill and Wesley take the resurrection as plain, Wesley noting that no despairing speech is heard afterwards, showing what new life these words gave. Ellicott is careful: the verses may not teach the doctrine directly, yet they express the faith for which a resurrection is the only natural justification, a living trust in a personal God who cannot leave his holy one in corruption; a man may hold an opinion about rising and not believe in God, and there he differs from Job. Keil and Delitzsch rule out the rival reading, finding here no hope of bodily recovery; Clarke reports a third proposal, a coming vindication out of that wasted body, and rejects it.

The kinsman is explained from the law. Henry and Wesley rehearse the office of the next of kin — to buy back a mortgaged inheritance, avenge a death, keep a name alive — and apply it: an estate mortgaged by sin, a debt paid, death's contriver destroyed in his own kingdom. Clarke restricts the title to one of the same kindred; Gill arrives there by elimination, barring any human vindicator, since no man stands on earth at the latter day, and barring the Father, seldom so titled and never standing here. Ellicott counts the earlier speeches that wanted a daysman, a witness in heaven, an advocate, a surety, and finds him past wanting: God will take those offices himself, the Goel being real already, however future his appearing. Bildad had threatened him with the extinction of his memory; he appeals instead to later ages, and Ellicott observes that we who still argue the sentence show how that appeal has fared.

Four readings of the standing-place come from two words. Ellicott keeps them literal, upon dust, citing the identical idiom in the chapter on leviathan against the version over the dust. Clarke takes precisely that version, the dust being the dead, the figure one arising above those who sleep in it. Wesley has him on the grave, a conquered enemy underfoot; Henry on the dust to which this earth will itself be reduced. On the skin, Gill makes it the grave's work rather than the ulcers', the frame stripped at last of flesh and bone; Clarke makes disease the destroyer and its object no body but a wretched composition of misery; Keil and Delitzsch render a seeing of God without flesh, where Henry, Wesley and Gill require eyes of flesh in a glorified body; Ellicott allows the first reference to be a present sight, held against the corruption already at work. Henry handles the decay carelessly, pointing at the wasted limbs — call it what you will, it will shortly feed worms — and says the rising shines brighter for it, the power that made a body of common dust being able to raise it from its own. The last clause he reads as every desire summed into one; Ellicott notes where the Church set the confession, at the head of the office for burying the dead.
28:
The confession turns outward. Gill states the purpose simply: having said what he believes, the sufferer tells the three what use to make of it. Clarke prefers a future to a conditional — then ye shall say — and borrows a sharper version of the question from Good, in which they stand already convinced: how did we persecute him, and we now see we did wrong.

In whom it is found depends on a variant Clarke thinks decisive. Against the received in me he sets in him, read by over a hundred manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi and by several versions, turning the clause from a confession into a verdict passed on Job by his accusers. Henry quotes that form without argument; Gill, Wesley and Ellicott keep the first person.

What the phrase names is the real division, and Ellicott puts the fork plainly: either the cause of the suffering or the substance of godliness. He takes the first, reading the sentence as the three arguing backwards from the calamity — why should God strike any man without cause, so the cause must lie in this one. The others take the second. Henry makes it a living, quickening, commanding principle of grace, as needful to religion as a root to a tree, which owes to it both fixedness and fruit; love to God and to a brother, faith, a hatred of sin are what he means, all else being leaves beside. Wesley compresses it: all true religion begins in living faith. Clarke describes a pure practice and a sound hope standing on a sound faith received from God himself.

Henry turns that definition into a rule of charity before he turns to the threat. Each is to see the principle rooted in himself, and to believe that many hold it who are not in everything of his mind, who have their follies and weaknesses; and it is at his peril if he troubles such a man. Job and the three differed over providence and agreed in believing another world, which should have kept them from harrying one another.

All of them read the sword as a judgment, though they differ on whose hand holds it. Gill excludes the magistrate and the invader from the primary sense, leaving the avenging edge of divine justice, lest the glittering blade be whetted and the hand take hold to requite the innocent — though human instruments may serve that end. Henry runs the two together: a censorious temper breeds the kind of crime that brings men under the magistrate, and God often avenges it himself, since those who showed no mercy shall find none. Wesley keeps it general, some considerable judgment called a sword as in the song of Moses, and takes the warning as kindly meant, given in time to be prevented. Clarke is plainer: the anger they displayed God will resent and punish.

The closing words carry the weight of the argument. Clarke draws a proof from them rather than a threat, reasoning that the unequal division of wealth and want, health and sickness, in this life is itself evidence that a reckoning must come in which evil is punished and virtue rewarded. Henry says as much with the stress on speech: there is not only a government now but a reckoning later, where hard words must be answered for, and good men need the terrors of the Almighty to frighten them off rash judging. Wesley puts it in a line, that God observes and will judge all their words and actions. Ellicott notes the irony: the punishment held over them is the one of which they had taken this man for a conspicuous instance. Clarke adds one argument for the vindication reading he had already declined, that a hope full of immortality sits awkwardly with a man who has cursed the day of his birth.
